questions.text: Let [latex] Z_n [/latex] be the group of integers [latex] \{0,1,2, \ldots, n-1\} [/latex] with addition modulo [latex] n [/latex] as the group operation. The number of elements in the group [latex] Z_2 \times Z_3 \times Z_4 [/latex] that are their own inverses is
questions.solution:
[latex](a,b,c)[/latex] is its own inverse iff [latex]2a\equiv0\ (\text{mod }2)[/latex], [latex]2b\equiv0\ (\text{mod }3)[/latex], [latex]2c\equiv0\ (\text{mod }4)[/latex].

- [latex]Z_2[/latex]: a = 0, 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 choices
- [latex]Z_3[/latex]: b = 0 only [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1 choice
- [latex]Z_4[/latex]: c = 0, 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 choices

Total [latex]=2\times1\times2=4[/latex]

Answer: 4

questions.text: The chromatic number of a graph is the minimum number of colours used in a proper colouring of the graph. The chromatic number of the following graph is _______
questions.solution:
Number the 8 vertices 1 to 8 around the octagon.

- The 8 outer sides join consecutive vertices (odd-even).
- Every inner line (the 2 vertical, 2 horizontal and 4 slanted lines) joins two vertices 3 steps apart around the octagon, which is again one odd and one even vertex.

So colour odd vertices with colour 1 and even vertices with colour 2: no edge has both ends the same colour. The graph is bipartite, and it has edges, so it needs at least 2 colours.

Answer: 2

questions.text:
Let [latex] P [/latex] be the partial order defined on the set [latex] \{1,2,3,4\} [/latex] as follows
[latex] P=\{(x, x) \mid x \in\{1,2,3,4\}\} \cup\{(1,2),(3,2),(3,4)\} [/latex]
The number of total orders on [latex] \{1,2,3,4\} [/latex] that contain [latex] P [/latex] is ______
questions.solution:
A total order containing P must keep [latex]1 \lt 2,\ 3 \lt 2,\ 3 \lt 4[/latex]. Count such orderings (linear extensions).

The first element must be 1 or 3 (nothing must come before them).
- Start with 1: next must be 3 (both 2 and 4 need 3 first), then 2, 4 in any order [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1324, 1342 (2 orders).
- Start with 3: arrange 1, 2, 4 with 1 before 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3124, 3142, 3412 (3 orders).

Total = 5

Answer: 5

questions.text:
When six unbiased dice are rolled simultaneously, the probability of getting all
distinct numbers (i.e., 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6) is
questions.solution:
Total outcomes [latex]=6^6=46656[/latex].
All distinct means the six dice show 1-6 in some order: [latex]6!=720[/latex] outcomes.

[latex]P=\dfrac{720}{46656}=\dfrac{5}{324}[/latex]

Answer: [latex]\frac{5}{324}[/latex]

questions.text: Let [latex] A  [/latex] be the adjacency matrix of a simple undirected graph [latex]G[/latex]. Suppose [latex]A[/latex] is its own inverse. Which one of the following statements is always TRUE?
questions.solution:
[latex]A=A^{-1}\Rightarrow A^2=I[/latex].

- [latex](A^2)_{ii}[/latex] = degree of vertex [latex]i[/latex] = 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] every vertex has exactly one neighbour.
- [latex](A^2)_{ij}=0[/latex] for [latex]i\ne j[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] consistent with that.

A graph where every vertex has degree exactly 1 is a set of disjoint edges covering all vertices [latex]\text{---}[/latex] a perfect matching.

Answer: G is a perfect matching
